title: Local multiplets, effective-chain dynamics, and momentum reconstruction in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg pentamer chain

Clusterized quantum spin chains connect local few-spin multiplets to extended many-body excitations. We investigate a spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain with a five-site unit cell by combining exact diagonalization, low-energy projection, finite-size density-matrix renormalization group calculations, entanglement diagnostics, correction-vector spectra, and real-time matrix-product-state dynamics. For positive intra-cell and inter-cell couplings, the isolated pentamer retains an even-reflection-parity spin-1/2 ground-state doublet. Projecting the inter-cell exchange onto this doublet gives an antiferromagnetic effective Heisenberg chain, and both two-pentamer exact diagonalization and finite-chain calculations show that the leading correction to the projected energy is quadratic in the inter-cell coupling. Matched-size entanglement estimates, small finite-size spin gaps, algebraic correlations, and a dominant response at $q=\pi$ are consistent with a $c=1$ effective-chain description at the tested positive-coupling points, without establishing such behavior over the entire coupling plane. Reflection parity suppresses the lowest excited doublet at $q=\pi$, whereas spin-3/2 multiplets carry 84.1%--97.6% of the isolated-pentamer inelastic weight. Independently validated correction-vector and time-evolution calculations connect these local selection rules to the collective spectrum. In the negative-$\alpha$ region, 96 parameter--size records at 48 coupling points were evaluated, of which 89 passed the Practical V2 gates and seven remained bounded. A further 29 $L=60,80$ refinement cells passed the complete numerical and provenance chain. The dominant finite-size momentum reconstructs from approximately $0.60\pi$ to $\pi$, but none of eight candidate intervals satisfies the predeclared momentum and finite-size-flow criteria simultaneously. A final $k=8\rightarrow12$ Krylov-subspace control at the most solver-sensitive $L=80$ point leaves $q_{peak}/\pi=1$ unchanged and changes the spin gap, dominant ratio, and entropy by at most $7.6\times10^{-12}$, $8.4\times10^{-8}$, and $5.8\times10^{-8}$, respectively. We therefore identify a robust finite-size momentum reconstruction, retain crossover as the working interpretation, and withhold a separate thermodynamic phase label.

Clusterized quantum magnets provide a direct route from the spectrum of a few-spin unit to the collective behavior of a quantum many-body system. Their local multiplets can survive as low-energy degrees of freedom, become dispersive, or be removed from an experimental response by symmetry. This makes clusterized chains useful for disentangling three questions that are often mixed together in a conventional phase diagram: which local state is active, how neighboring units couple, and which resulting excitations are actually visible.

The recent spin-1/2 tetramer chain study provides a useful reference because it treats magnetic order, entanglement structure, and excitation spectra within a common coupling diagram [1]. Replacing four spins by five is not, however, a minor geometric modification. A unit cell with an odd number of half-integer spins retains a half-integer degree of freedom unless symmetry breaking or ground-state degeneracy intervenes. Lieb--Schultz--Mattis-type results therefore constrain a unique symmetry-preserving gapped ground state under the relevant translation and spin-rotation assumptions [4,5]. The constraint is important, but it does not determine the phase diagram and does not by itself prove a globally gapless $c=1$ state.

Here we study a linear Heisenberg pentamer chain with two intra-cell exchanges, $J_1$ and $J_2$, and an inter-cell exchange $J_3$. We set $J_1=1$ and write $\alpha=J_2/J_1$ and $\beta=J_3/J_1$. The geometry differs from previously studied mixed-spin or differently connected pentamers, so their multiplet assignments are not transferred to the present model [2]. Instead, we determine the complete isolated-cell spectrum, construct the low-energy projected chain, and test the resulting picture against static and dynamical many-body calculations.

Three results organize the paper. First, throughout the sampled positive-$\alpha$ region, the pentamer ground state is an even-parity spin-1/2 doublet and positive $\beta$ generates an antiferromagnetic effective chain. Second, reflection parity makes the lowest excited doublet essentially dark at $q=\pi$ and concentrates the local inelastic weight in spin-3/2 multiplets. Third, negative $\alpha$ produces a reproducible finite-size reconstruction of the dominant momentum. The last result is not promoted to a thermodynamic phase boundary because two independently declared diagnostics do not localize the same adjacent interval.

This distinction between a resolved microscopic mechanism and a bounded phase-diagram statement is central to our analysis. All production records are accepted only after numerical, transfer, checksum, and independent-validator gates. We show the raw spectral ringing rather than clipping it, distinguish the Krylov dimension $k$ from the matrix-product-state bond dimension $\chi$, and report initial-state differences as systematic sensitivity rather than statistical uncertainty. The resulting evidence supports an odd-unit-cell route from local multiplets to collective dynamics while defining precisely which conclusions cannot be inherited from the tetramer problem.

blocks.text: 2.2 Static finite-chain calculations and acceptance gates

Finite chains use open boundaries and $L=5N$ physical spins. Ground states are obtained in fixed total-$S^z$ sectors with density-matrix renormalization group calculations in a matrix-product-state representation [7,8]. Sector-specific initial states are used rather than assuming that a single initialization samples all low-energy solutions.

The positive-region data set contains 105 accepted records at $L=40,60,80$. For negative $\alpha$, the Practical V2 protocol uses two product-state initializations, `center` and `ferro_j2`, in the $S^z=0$ sector and a fixed `center` initialization in the $S^z=1$ sector. A new record is accepted only if the variance per site is no larger than $5\times10^{-8}$, the final truncation error is no larger than $10^{-9}$, the measured magnetization satisfies $|S^z-S^z_{target}|\leq10^{-8}$, and the sector gap is no smaller than $-10^{-8}$. New Practical V2 runs use no more than 64 sweeps. The two $S^z=0$ initial states test initialization sensitivity; they are not independent statistical replicates.

Every accepted remote result is checked by a parent manifest and child checksums, transferred without overwriting an earlier run, checked again locally, and passed through an independent validator. Results that fail a gate are retained as bounded or not evaluable and are excluded from accepted-only boundary inference. This procedure is deliberately stricter than the visual smoothness of a plotted curve.
2.3 Entanglement, correlation, and momentum diagnostics
For an open critical chain, the bond entropy is compared with the conformal form

The intercept $a_g$ depends on the bond class $g=b\bmod5$ or $b\bmod10$, while a common slope defines the descriptive coefficient $c_{eff}$. Fits use central windows $fL\leq b\leq(1-f)L$ with $f=0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25$. We call this quantity an effective entropy coefficient rather than a central charge unless size and solver controls justify the stronger language [6]. Correlation envelopes, finite-size sector gaps, the static structure factor, and connected bond--bond correlations provide complementary diagnostics.

The negative-$\alpha$ scan tracks the dominant structure-factor momentum $q_{peak}$ and a dominant-ratio observable $R_L$. Candidate boundaries were declared only when an adjacent coupling interval showed both a momentum reconstruction and a consistent finite-size signature in $\Delta R=R_{80}-R_{60}$. A momentum change without the corresponding $\Delta R$ condition is reported as finite-size reconstruction, not a phase boundary.
2.4 Dynamical structure factor

We compute the dynamical structure factor by two independent matrix-product-state routes. Correction-vector DMRG gives a fixed-frequency spectrum at $q=\pi$ [10]. Real-time evolution followed by Fourier transformation provides the full momentum dependence and an independent line-shape check [9,11]. The correction-vector implementation first reproduces the complete $L=10$ spectrum with relative $L_2$ error $8.52\times10^{-12}$.

The production full-momentum calculations use $L=40$, $t_{\max}=30$, 121 momentum points, 301 frequency points, and paired time steps $\Delta t=0.025$ and 0.0125. The raw Fourier matrices, including negative ringing from the finite time window, are retained and tested rather than clipped. The accepted correction-vector/time-evolution comparison is limited to the historical $q=\pi$, $\eta=0.1$ slice and its open-boundary normalization and spatial-window approximation; it is not a full-momentum correction-vector claim.
2.5 Krylov-subspace stability control

The saved-state anomaly at $(\alpha,\beta)=(-0.10,0.25)$ was the point most sensitive to the local eigensolver configuration. We therefore performed a terminal $L=80$ control in which all physical and DMRG settings were held fixed while the Krylov dimension was increased from $k=8$ to $k=12$. Both `center` and `ferro_j2` initial states used 64 sweeps, maximum configured bond dimension 1200, cutoff $10^{-11}$, and the same 401-point momentum grid. Here $k$ is the Krylov-subspace dimension and must not be confused with the MPS bond dimension $\chi$.

The $k=12$ run passed the remote and local checksum chain and the Practical V2 validator. Its variance per site was $1.86$--$1.87\times10^{-11}$, and the two sector gaps were $7.2772047002\times10^{-5}$ and $7.2772051798\times10^{-5}$. Across 172 matched records, the $k=8\rightarrow12$ differences were bounded by $7.5211\times10^{-12}$ for the spin gap, $8.3994\times10^{-8}$ for the dominant ratio, and $5.7413\times10^{-8}$ for the entropy; $q_{peak}/\pi$ remained 1. This audit closes the Krylov-stability question at one finite-size point, but it is not a bond-dimension sweep or a thermodynamic extrapolation.
3.1 An odd pentamer retains a low-energy spin doublet

At all 100 sampled points with $0<\alpha\leq1$, the isolated pentamer ground state is an even-reflection-parity spin-1/2 doublet. The lowest excited doublet is odd under reflection, whereas the lowest spin-3/2 multiplet is even. The five-spin unit therefore retains an active half-integer degree of freedom instead of forming a fully quenched singlet cluster.

At $\alpha=0.14$, 0.23, and 0.33, the projected coupling satisfies $J_{eff}/\beta=0.4396$, 0.4318, and 0.4189, respectively. Positive $\beta$ thus generates an antiferromagnetic effective spin-1/2 chain. The residual between projected and exact ground-state energies scales with powers 1.9689--1.9915 for two coupled pentamers and 1.9483--1.9495 for complete chains with $N=8,12,16$. The leading correction is therefore consistent with the expected $O(\beta^2)$ term.

items.caption: Figure 2. Positive-alpha multiplet flow and the reflection-parity filter at q=pi. The lowest excited doublet is dark, whereas even-parity spin-3/2 multiplets dominate the local inelastic response.

blocks.text: 3.2 Positive couplings support one resolved effective-chain regime

The strict positive-region mesh contains 105 accepted records. The $L=40,60,80$ finite-size diagnostic does not produce a stable interior crossing: all accepted interior size differences retain the same sign under leave-one-out and weakest-point audits. This is a bounded negative result. It establishes that the present data resolve no internal boundary in $0\leq\alpha,\beta\leq1$; it does not prove that every thermodynamic point belongs to one phase.

The low-energy observables provide an independent interpretation. At $\alpha=0.23$ and weak inter-cell coupling, matched-size entanglement estimators give $c_{eff}=1.0240$--1.0331 relative to an open spin-1/2 Heisenberg-chain oracle. Finite-size spin gaps extrapolate close to zero, the correlation envelope has exponents 0.95--0.98, and the static structure factor is dominated by $q=\pi$. Taken together, these results are consistent with a gapless antiferromagnetic effective chain at the tested points, rather than a gapped tetramer-like cluster phase [12].

items.caption: Figure 3. Positive-region ground-state diagnostics. The dense map is exploratory, while the strict 105-record L=40,60,80 mesh provides the accepted crossing test; no stable internal bracket is resolved.

Figure 4. Entanglement and finite-size low-energy diagnostics. The five inequivalent bond classes are calibrated against a matched-size c=1 Heisenberg-chain oracle, so the plotted coefficient is interpreted only at the tested points.

blocks.text: 3.3 Reflection parity selects the visible local excitation

The lowest excited doublet is not the lowest visible $q=\pi$ excitation. Its projector-resolved spectral weight is below $4.6\times10^{-27}$ at the three representative positive-$\alpha$ points because the $q=\pi$ spin operator is even under reflection whereas the target doublet is odd. The lowest even-parity spin-3/2 multiplet carries a weight of approximately 0.325--0.333, and all spin-3/2 multiplets together account for 84.1%--97.6% of the isolated-pentamer inelastic response.

This result supplies a microscopic selection rule for the extended-chain spectrum. It does not assume that an isolated spin-3/2 multiplet remains a sharp quasiparticle at finite $\beta$; instead, it identifies which local sector can contribute when collective states are formed.

items.caption: Figure 5. Effective-chain continuum and local selection rules. The continuum bounds describe the weak-coupling effective chain, while the isolated-pentamer weights identify bright local spin-3/2 channels without assigning an unvalidated quasiparticle label.

blocks.text: 3.4 Collective dynamics confirms the pointwise spectral picture

At $(\alpha,\beta,L,q)=(0.23,0.5,40,\pi)$, eleven accepted correction-vector frequencies cover $0\leq\omega/J_1\leq1.5$ and pass the peak-bracketing, spectral-weight, and residual gates. The line shape agrees with the independently converged time-evolution result within the declared peak-position and integrated-weight budgets.

Full-momentum time evolution was completed at $(\alpha,\beta)=(1,1)$, $(1,0.1)$, and $(0.23,0.5)$. All six individual runs and all three $\Delta t$/$\Delta t/2$ pairs passed. The global and $q=\pi$ peak drifts are 0, 0, and $0.01J_1$ for the uniform, weak-coupling, and agreement points. The corresponding low-frequency integrated-weight changes are $4.32\times10^{-5}$, $2.74\times10^{-5}$, and $1.97\times10^{-5}$.

The uniform point uses broadening $\eta=0.1$, whereas the weak-coupling and agreement points use $\eta=0.2$; all three use a spatial window of 18 sites. We therefore compare the organization and time-step stability of the panels, but not weak-peak linewidths across different broadenings. The three points form production spectral evidence, not a dense dynamical phase diagram.

items.caption: Figure 6. Raw full-momentum Szz(q,omega) and paired q=pi time-step slices at three representative positive-coupling points. Negative Fourier ringing is shown rather than clipped; all six runs and all three dt/dt2 pairs pass their spectral gates.

Figure 7. Pointwise correction-vector and time-evolution comparison at alpha=0.23, beta=0.5, L=40, and q=pi. Eleven accepted frequencies bracket the principal feature and cover omega/J1 from 0 to 1.5.

blocks.text: 3.5 Negative intra-cell exchange produces a finite-size momentum reconstruction

The negative-$\alpha$ data show a reproducible change in the dominant structure-factor momentum. Deep in the scanned region, $q_{peak}\simeq0.60\pi$; closer to $\alpha=0$, the maximum locks to $q=\pi$. Stage B evaluated 96 parameter--size records at 48 coupling points. Eighty-nine records passed the Practical V2 gates, while seven non-boundary records remained bounded and were excluded from accepted-only inference.

The accepted-only analysis identified eight candidate intervals across seven $\beta$ slices. Stage C evaluated these intervals with 29 additional $L=60,80$ cells at 64 sweeps. All 29 cells passed the remote parent and child checksums, non-overwriting transfer, local checksum, and independent validator. Seven of eight targets retain either a momentum reconstruction or a sign change in $\Delta R=R_{80}-R_{60}$ that meets its declared diagnostic criterion. No adjacent interval, however, carries both signatures. Only the $\beta=0.05$ momentum interval reaches the target width 0.025, and the $\beta=0.10$ slice supplies no supported internal interval at the final size pair.

The data therefore establish a finite-size momentum reconstruction but do not locate a joint thermodynamic boundary. The mismatch is compatible with a broad crossover, a slowly converging incommensurate regime, or residual finite-size effects. Distinguishing these possibilities requires a different discriminating observable or substantially larger controlled sizes, not simply more points on the same grid.

items.caption: Figure 8. Accepted-only negative-alpha momentum reconstruction. Large-size data move from q_peak about 0.60pi to pi, but the momentum and dominant-ratio diagnostics do not select the same adjacent interval.

blocks.text: 3.6 Saved-state diagnostics and the terminal solver control

Six additional points were evaluated with saved $L=80$ ground-state wavefunctions using two $S^z=0$ initial states and 64 sweeps per initial state. The points were $\alpha=-0.25,-0.175,-0.10$ at $\beta=0.25$ and $\alpha=-0.625,-0.50,-0.425$ at $\beta=0.75$. All parent runs passed the Practical V2 gates, with a largest variance per site of $1.2875\times10^{-9}$. Numerical acceptance alone did not determine their thermodynamic phase.

At $\beta=0.25$, the earlier $L=80$ audit gave $c_{eff}=0.467$--0.605 at $\alpha=-0.10$, compared with 0.886--0.971 at $\alpha=-0.175$ and 0.981--1.049 at $\alpha=-0.25$. The three $\beta=0.75$ points gave 0.905--0.976. These ranges measure sensitivity to the fitting window and initialization; they are not confidence intervals.

A subsequent size comparison used $L=40,60,80$ at $\alpha=-0.175,-0.150,-0.125,-0.100$ and $\beta=0.25$. At $\alpha=-0.10$, the ten-intercept coefficients span 0.970--1.340, 0.625--0.959, and 0.467--0.605 with increasing length. At fixed window $f=0.20$, the dual-start mean decreases from 0.988 to 0.695 and 0.533. Because only $N=8,12,16$ pentamers are available, this strong size dependence cannot be identified with a thermodynamic central charge. Same-class bond differences and connected inter-cell bond correlations also decrease over these sizes, but the available separations neither establish nor exclude a nonzero long-range order parameter.

items.caption: Figure 9. Joint finite-size evidence near the negative-alpha anomaly. Entropy coefficients, bond-class variation, connected correlations, and sector gaps are displayed together to expose size and initialization sensitivity.

blocks.text: The terminal Krylov control clarifies which part of this anomaly was numerical. The earlier $k=3\rightarrow8$ change strongly revised some entropy slopes at $\alpha=-0.10$, showing that the old solver setting was not stable. By contrast, the final $k=8\rightarrow12$ comparison at the same $L=80$ point is stable to the small absolute differences quoted in Section 2.5 and leaves $q_{peak}=\pi$. This makes the accepted $L=80$ observables at that point robust against a further increase of the Krylov subspace. It still does not supply a $\chi$ series, larger system sizes, or a thermodynamic order parameter. Accordingly, the anomaly remains a localized, numerically credible finite-size feature rather than evidence for a new phase.
4.1 Why the pentamer differs from the tetramer

The main contrast with the reference tetramer follows from unit-cell parity. Four spin-1/2 degrees of freedom can form an integer-spin or singlet cluster sector. Five leave a half-integer degree of freedom unless translation symmetry is broken or the ground state is degenerate. In the tested positive-$\alpha$ pentamer points, the surviving doublet converts the inter-cell exchange into an antiferromagnetic interaction between effective spins. The finite-size data are therefore consistent with a critical effective chain, whereas the tetramer phase names and its local triplon, quarton, or higher composite labels cannot be transferred by geometric analogy alone [1].

The spectral comparison sharpens this distinction. The pentamer's odd-parity excited doublet is dark at $q=\pi$, while higher even-parity spin-3/2 sectors remain bright. In the chain, that hierarchy coexists with a dispersive low-energy continuum and five-site folding or high-energy structure. The local multiplet analysis thus predicts visibility, while the many-body calculation determines whether the weight forms a continuum, a broadened branch, or a more complex folded response.
4.2 Controlled interpretation near alpha=0

For $|\alpha|≪\min(1,\beta)$, a trimer--dimer decomposition gives a useful limiting picture. Projecting the trimer doublets and eliminating the inter-cell dimer triplet produces the candidate exchange

An eight-spin trimer--dimer--trimer oracle evaluated at 47 points supports this local $\alpha^2/\beta$ scaling in its asymptotic domain, consistent with the effective-spin logic of verified trimer-chain work [3]. The finite-$\alpha$ controls at $(-0.10,0.25)$ and $(-0.175,0.25)$ deviate from the leading term by $-36.1351\%$ and $-53.8550\%$, respectively. These are signed deviations of a local controlled approximation, not numerical errors in the $L=80$ calculation. The open-boundary sector gap also need not equal a bulk excitation gap. The decomposition therefore provides a mechanism close to $\alpha=0$, not proof of a second phase or a global $c=1$ region.
4.3 What the negative-alpha data establish

The negative-$\alpha$ scan answers a narrower but reproducible question: the dominant finite-size momentum changes across the coupling plane. It does not yet answer whether that change sharpens into a Lifshitz transition, belongs to a broad incommensurate regime, or remains a finite-size crossover. The decisive limitation is not a failed DMRG convergence test. The accepted Stage C cells pass the numerical and provenance gates, and the most sensitive endpoint passes the $k=8\rightarrow12$ solver control. The limitation is physical: the momentum and finite-size-flow diagnostics do not identify the same boundary interval.

This separation matters for scientific interpretation. Numerical convergence validates the state and measured observables at a finite size; it cannot manufacture agreement between physically distinct diagnostics. Conversely, the absence of a joint boundary does not prove that the entire negative region is a single phase. Our conservative conclusion is therefore positive rather than merely inconclusive: the finite-size momentum reconstruction is established, while a separately named thermodynamic phase is not.
4.4 Scope and remaining tests

The present work establishes the local multiplet mechanism, positive-coupling effective-chain dynamics at selected points, and a bounded negative-coupling reconstruction. It does not provide a complete thermodynamic phase diagram. A stronger phase claim would require at least one observable with a controlled large-size singularity or crossing that is consistent with the momentum reconstruction, together with an effective bond-dimension series at the most sensitive points. A negative-$\alpha$ dynamical representative could test whether the momentum reorganization is accompanied by a qualitative spectral transfer, but such a calculation would strengthen the phenomenology rather than by itself prove a phase boundary.

We have traced the behavior of a spin-1/2 Heisenberg pentamer chain from its isolated local multiplets to its collective response. At the tested positive couplings, the pentamer retains an even-parity spin-1/2 doublet, positive inter-cell exchange generates an antiferromagnetic effective chain, and the leading projection error is quadratic in the inter-cell coupling. Entanglement, finite-size gaps, correlations, and static structure factors are consistent with a $c=1$ effective-chain description at those points. Reflection parity makes the lowest excited doublet dark at $q=\pi$ and shifts most local inelastic weight into spin-3/2 sectors. Correction-vector and real-time calculations then connect this local selection rule to validated collective spectra.

On the negative-$\alpha$ side, the accepted-only campaign reveals a reconstruction from $q_{peak}\simeq0.60\pi$ to $q=\pi$. All 29 final refinement cells pass the full numerical and provenance chain, and a terminal $k=8\rightarrow12$ control shows that the most sensitive $L=80$ endpoint is stable with respect to a larger Krylov subspace. Nevertheless, none of the eight candidate intervals satisfies the momentum and dominant-ratio criteria simultaneously. We therefore report a robust finite-size momentum reconstruction and retain crossover as the working interpretation, while deliberately withholding a new phase name. The resulting distinction between an established microscopic mechanism, production-level dynamics, and a bounded phase statement is the central conclusion of this work.
